result: The authors demonstrate that thermal stress at 40°C induces disassembly of existing Sup35 amyloid in [PSI+]Weak strains. SDS-resistant Sup35 aggregates are reduced in size immediately following thermal stress and completely lost after recovery, with over 70% becoming detergent sensitive, indicating Hsp104-mediated amyloid disassembly.
evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 3 explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors convincingly demonstrate that heat-induced aggregates of proteins other than Sup35 asymmetrically retain Hsp104...and thereby increase Hsp104 concentration in mother cells to a level that allows Sup35 disaggregation.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Hsp104 dissolves Sup35 prions that encode weak [PSI+] at elevated temperatures' and acknowledges 'it has already been shown in vitro that Hsp104 can rapidly dissolve Sup35 prions.'

result: Chemical inhibition of Hsp104 with GdnHCl or reducing its dosage through heterozygous disruption reduced [PSI+]Weak curing by more than 50%, demonstrating Hsp104's role in prion curing.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges this evidence, stating 'Evidence for involvement of Hsp104 in Sup35 amyloid disassembly comes both from the literature and new data presented here, that (i) the GdnHCl curing of [PSI+]Weak and a ∼50% decrease in curing efficiency was observed in a heterozygous deletion of Hsp104.' This establishes necessity but reviewers note it does not establish sufficiency.

result: At elevated temperatures, Hsp104-GFP localizes to cytoplasmic foci containing heat-induced aggregates (including model substrate luciferase-mCherry), with the amount of co-immunocaptured proteins correlating with aggregate accumulation and curing efficiency. GdnHCl treatment reduces this association and curing efficiency.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the localization data but express concerns about the correlative nature of the evidence. Reviewer 1 requests 'Is it possible to demonstrate this specific interaction, e.g. by co-immunoprecipitation?' Reviewer 2 states 'An important conclusion is that the heat-induced aggregates directly retain Hsp104, but there is no evidence for the direct interaction between these two factors, other than strong correlation' and requests isolation of aggregates to demonstrate Hsp104 binding. Reviewer 3 notes 'A limitation is that several conclusions are based upon correlative evidence.'

result: Hsp104-GFP is asymmetrically retained in mother cells following thermal stress, with retention increasing progressively with temperature (60% at 30°C to 75% at 40°C). This asymmetric retention correlates with curing efficiency, and disruption of BNI1 reduces both Hsp104 retention and curing. Mother cells accumulating Hsp104 are more likely to be cured than daughters.
evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 3 explicitly support this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'The concept that the (temporary) sequestration of important proteostasis factors into an aggregate can be beneficial instead of detrimental is novel and exciting' and notes the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' asymmetric retention. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'asymmetric Hsp104 retention by heat induced, non-prion aggregates in late cell cycle-stage cells, leads to high enough Hsp104 levels to promote dissolution of Sup35 prions.' The spatiotemporal mechanism is recognized as novel.

result: Cell cycle stage determines curing sensitivity. Cells arrested with nocodazole (late cell cycle) show bimodal Hsp104-GFP distribution and nearly quantitative curing (~90%) at 40°C, while α-factor arrested cells (early cell cycle) show normal distribution and inefficient curing (~15%). Curing occurs most efficiently when late-stage cells are exposed to elevated temperature.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern about the nocodazole experiments: 'The use of nocodazole in Figure 5 seems problematic as it may influence several other pathways that are involved in the formation and degradation of aggregates. Since the cell cycle analysis is not contributing critically to the overall model, it might be better to remove this section, or move it to the supplement.' This suggests the reviewer questions whether the cell cycle dependency is sufficiently established or whether confounding effects exist.

result: Protein aggregates accumulate independent of prion status at elevated temperatures, with accumulation severity dependent on temperature (10% at 37°C, 40% at 40°C). This accumulation correlates with curing efficiency, though GdnHCl treatment reduces curing without reducing aggregate accumulation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises methodological concerns: 'The protocol used for differential centrifugation is not sufficiently well described...Since the quantification of these aggregates is an important aspect of this story, the authors should quantify aggregate formation with more vigor, using alternative procedures such as sucrose-density gradients and ultra-centrifugation.' The reviewer also requests 'the differential accumulation of aggregates in mother vs. daughter cells should be quantified.' This indicates uncertainty about the robustness of the aggregate quantification.

result: Neither Sup35 nor chaperone expression levels correlate with curing efficiency. Hsp104 overexpression alone induces only ~40% curing (vs ~95% with thermal stress) and increases aggregate size rather than promoting disassembly, indicating thermal stress and chaperone overexpression induce distinct changes.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that overexpression data is 'currently not shown (p.18)' and requests the authors 'showing the over-expression data...that establishes that the o/e of Hsp104 alone, to the same level achieved in this study through its asymmetric retention, suffices to induce curing.' This indicates the comparison between thermal stress and overexpression effects needs stronger experimental support.

result: [PSI+]Weak (thermodynamically stable but less efficiently amplified) is cured at elevated temperature while [PSI+]Strong is not. Reducing [PSI+]Strong amplification by expressing Sup35 mutant G58D or reducing Sup35 expression promotes curing, indicating amyloid amplification rather than stability limits clearance.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding: 'Upon recognizing this potential mechanism, the authors then cleverly tweak the system to enable curing of Sup35 prions that encode strong [PSI+].' The reviewers do not challenge this result, and it is presented as a key insight into the determinants of amyloid clearance.

result: Blocking Hsp104 ATPase activity after thermal stress with GdnHCl does not reduce Hsp104-GFP localization to foci or asymmetric retention, but reduces curing by nearly 50%, demonstrating both Hsp104 localization and activity are required for curing.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors convincingly demonstrate that heat-induced aggregates of proteins other than Sup35 asymmetrically retain Hsp104 during cell division, in a process that is dependent of the enzymatic activity of Hsp104.' The GdnHCl experiments after thermal stress support the requirement for both localization and activity, though reviewers request more direct demonstration of the interaction.

result: Nearly 100% of cells contain Hsp104-GFP foci immediately after thermal stress, but only ~80% retain foci when division re-initiates. Unbudded cells resolve foci before division (60%), while budded cells retain foci through division (~8% resolved), indicating Hsp104 retention depends on inability to resolve substrates before division.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this temporal analysis. Reviewer 1 states the paper 'provides insight into an unanticipated role of asymmetric cell division in protein aggregate management.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the spatiotemporal mechanism revealed by these studies is entirely novel.' The time-course data supporting substrate-chaperone dynamics is accepted as part of the overall model.

result: The increase in Hsp104 expression alone is insufficient for curing; rather, chaperone spatial engagement, substrate processing dynamics, and partitioning during cell division represent cell-based limitations on proteostasis capacity. Hsp104 engagement with heat-induced aggregates enhances proteostasis by increasing accumulation beyond gene expression changes.
evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 3 explicitly support this conceptual framework. Reviewer 1 states 'The concept that the (temporary) sequestration of important proteostasis factors into an aggregate can be beneficial instead of detrimental is novel and exciting.' Reviewer 3 notes 'this paper will raise awareness that spatiotemporal mechanisms can have a profound impact on proteostasis and amyloid resolution.' The overall model is accepted as a significant contribution.

result: Metazoans lack Hsp104 but have a conserved Hsp110/Hsp70/Hsp40 disaggregase system. This system is largely ineffective against amyloid in vitro but can promote slow disassembly with small heat shock proteins. Hsp110 localizes to foci and interacts with amyloids in vivo, suggesting potential similar mechanisms.
evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 raise concerns about broader relevance. Reviewer 2 states 'the use of Sup35 as a probe and the yeast cellular environment while highly relevant on its own, may not offer broadly relevant concepts than can be extrapolated to metazoans' and asks 'whether these concepts on Hsp104 are specific to yeast (which is still interesting) or can help us to understand the larger questions.' Reviewer 3 requests 'Some brief comments addressing this issue will allow the reader to comprehend the bigger picture.' The speculation about Hsp110 is noted but not validated.

result: Numerous cytoplasmic foci (aggresomes, IPOD, JUNQ, Q-bodies) arise in response to stressors. Q-bodies form under the mild thermal stress conditions used in this study. PQC factors localizing to these foci promote survival under stress.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests 'A broader context here would be useful as a number of laboratories have made observations on Q-bodies, iPOD, JUNQ, aggresomes' and notes these studies 'have demonstrated that aggregates have spatial restrictions and numerous papers have shown that multiple chaperones are associated with these aggregate structures.' The reviewers accept the existence of these structures but request better integration into the discussion.

result: Ssa1-GFP and Sis1-GFP localize to cytoplasmic foci at elevated temperature but are not asymmetrically retained following incubation at 40°C, unlike Hsp104, suggesting differential regulation of PQC factors.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this observation. It is presented as supporting evidence for the specificity of Hsp104 asymmetric retention. Reviewer 2 requests examination of 'other Hsp70 and Hsp40 isoforms' expression changes, but does not dispute the localization data for Ssa1 and Sis1.
